source_caption:
One Hundred and One Dalmatians (1961) is one of Disney’s most distinctive-looking films, and it’s not just because of all those adorable puppies. The movie actually changed the way Disney animation was produced.

Disney was facing a huge problem: how do you animate hundreds of dogs, each covered in dozens of spots, without spending years having every single detail traced by hand? The solution was xerography, a technique that allowed animators’ pencil drawings to be transferred directly onto animation cels.

That meant the artists’ original lines could finally appear on screen without being cleaned up and redrawn by hand. The result was a rougher, more expressive style that felt completely different from the polished look of earlier Disney classics.

The sketchy outlines, loose movement, and warm watercolor backgrounds gave the film a stylish, almost storybook-like look. Even Cruella de Vil’s sharp, angular design benefited from this new freedom.

The production was packed with impressive details. Artists created thousands of different spot patterns so the dogs wouldn’t all look identical, while long, flowing lines helped give each character a sense of movement and personality. The film also became an important financial success for Disney after the enormous cost of Sleeping Beauty.

What makes 101 Dalmatians still feel so fresh is that it never tries to hide the artists’ hands. You can see the pencil lines, the imperfections, and the energy in every frame. Instead of making the animation look perfectly polished, Disney let it feel alive — and that style has aged incredibly well.

source_details.synopsis: One Hundred and One Dalmatians (also known as 101 Dalmatians) is a 1961 American animated adventure comedy film produced by Walt Disney Productions with distribution by Buena Vista Distribution. Adapted from Dodie Smith's 1956 novel The Hundred and One Dalmatians, the film was directed by Hamilton Luske, Clyde Geronimi, and Wolfgang Reitherman in his feature-length directorial debut, from a script by Bill Peet. It features the voice talents of Rod Taylor, J. Pat O'Malley, Betty Lou Gerson, Martha Wentworth, Ben Wright, Cate Bauer, Dave Frankham, and Fred Worlock.
